Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. High rates of recidivism suggest that many people who go to prison end up committing another crime after they get out. — RECIDIVISM (n, không đếm được) = sự tái phạm; collocation thường gặp "a high rate of recidivism", "reduce/curb recidivism". Tránh viết "a recidivism" hay "recidivisms".

2. Some experts doubt that long prison terms actually act as an effective deterrent to crime. — DETERRENT (n) = yếu tố răn đe; collocation chuẩn là "act as a deterrent TO something", không dùng giới từ "for". Phân biệt với "deterrence" (khái niệm răn đe nói chung, trừu tượng hơn).

3. The heinous nature of the attack disturbed even experienced police officers. — HEINOUS (adj) = tàn bạo, ghê tởm đến mức gây sốc; thường đi với "crime/act/nature of something". Chỉ dùng cho hành vi cực kỳ nghiêm trọng, không dùng cho lỗi nhỏ.

4. Breaking into someone's house and stealing their belongings is a felony, not a minor offence. — FELONY (n) = trọng tội (phạt tù trên 1 năm); đối lập với "misdemeanour" (tội nhẹ). Học viên hay nhầm hai từ này khi phân loại mức độ nghiêm trọng của tội.

5. It is extremely difficult for a former prisoner to achieve full reintegration into society after release. — REINTEGRATION (n) = sự tái hoà nhập cộng đồng; collocation "reintegration into society", "a reintegration programme". Gốc "re- + integrate" giúp ghi nhớ nghĩa "hoà nhập trở lại".

6. Detectives spent months trying to identify the perpetrator of the crime. — PERPETRATOR (n) = thủ phạm, người trực tiếp gây án; collocation "the perpetrator of a crime", "identify/bring the perpetrator to justice". Đối lập với "victim" (nạn nhân).

7. Many criminologists believe that prisons should focus on the rehabilitation of offenders rather than simply punishing them. — REHABILITATION (n, không đếm được) = sự cải tạo; collocation "focus on rehabilitation", "rehabilitation, not retribution". Không nói "a rehabilitation".

8. Because it was his first offence, the court decided to give him a surprisingly lenient sentence. — LENIENT (adj) = khoan dung, nhẹ tay; collocation "a lenient sentence/judge". Đối lập với "strict/harsh". Danh từ liên quan là "leniency".

9. Years later, new evidence revealed that the man's conviction had been a miscarriage of justice. — MISCARRIAGE OF JUSTICE (n phrase) = án oan, sự bất công trong xét xử; collocation "a serious miscarriage of justice", "a victim of a miscarriage of justice". Đồng nghĩa "wrongful conviction".

10. In some neighbourhoods where the police are slow to respond, ordinary residents have started acting as vigilantes. — VIGILANTE (n) = người tự đứng ra thực thi pháp luật ngoài khuôn khổ chính thức; dễ nhầm về mặt chữ với "vigilant" (cảnh giác, tính từ) — hai từ không liên quan về nghĩa.

11. Critics argue that the new law is punitive rather than aimed at addressing the causes of offending. — PUNITIVE (adj) = mang tính trừng phạt; collocation "a punitive approach/measures". Đối lập với "rehabilitative/restorative".

12. Given how much damage the fraud caused, many felt that the company had merely been given a slap on the wrist. — A SLAP ON THE WRIST (idiom) = hình phạt rất nhẹ, mang tính cảnh cáo, không tương xứng với mức độ nghiêm trọng; thường dùng với động từ "get/give", không nói "do a slap on the wrist".

3. Band 7: Juvenile offenders should be dealt with differently from adult criminals within the justice system.
Band 8: Cases of juvenile delinquency arguably demand a distinct legal framework, given that young offenders are generally more amenable to rehabilitation than their adult counterparts.

6. Band 7: Supporting ex-offenders in securing steady employment can prevent them from reoffending.

7. Band 7: A court's verdict on guilt should always rest on solid, thoroughly examined evidence.
Band 8: Any verdict reached by a jury ought to be grounded in rigorously scrutinised evidence, lest an avoidable miscarriage of justice ensue.
8. Band 7: Some argue that prisons themselves can turn minor offenders into more serious criminals.
Band 8: Critics contend that custodial environments are themselves criminogenic, transforming petty offenders into hardened criminals rather than reforming them.

passages.text: When the first carefully randomised trials of restorative justice were published in the late 1990s, expectations among reformers ran high. The discipline of criminology had been searching for an approach that could lower reoffending without lengthening prison sentences, and conferencing — a structured meeting between offender, victim and trained facilitator — appeared to offer one. Two decades on, the evidence is, in the view of most reviewers, neither as dramatic as early advocates suggested nor as negligible as sceptics maintained. What the meta-analyses describe is a modest, fairly consistent reduction in repeat offending across a narrow band of cases, alongside a more substantial improvement in victims' reported sense of resolution. Disentangling those two findings has become the central methodological challenge of the field.

The most cited synthesis remains the Campbell Collaboration review co-authored by Lawrence Sherman of the University of Cambridge and Heather Strang of the Australian National University, who pooled data from ten randomised controlled trials in the United Kingdom and Australia between 1995 and 2004. Their headline estimate suggested that conferenced offenders committed roughly 27 per cent fewer further offences over the two years after the intervention than those processed through conventional courts. The figure has been widely circulated, although Sherman has cautioned that it reflects a particular sample: predominantly young, predominantly first-time offenders, and almost exclusively cases in which the victim had freely agreed to participate. Generalising beyond those conditions, he argues, is not warranted by the trials as designed.

A second tradition of scholarship, associated with the work of Daniel Woods and others at the Jerry Lee Centre, has reanalysed the same trials with a sharper focus on offence type. Their conclusion is that the apparent overall effect conceals considerable heterogeneity. Violent offences appear to respond rather better to conferencing than property offences, a pattern that the original trial designers had not predicted. One interpretation, advanced cautiously by Sherman in later papers, is that the emotional weight of a face-to-face encounter exerts greater leverage when the original harm was personal rather than financial. The proposition is plausible but, as Woods has observed, rests on a small number of trials and would benefit from replication in jurisdictions where conferencing is used for assault rather than burglary.

Other researchers have questioned the framework itself. Professor Carolyn Hoyle of the University of Oxford, while broadly sympathetic to the restorative project, has pointed out that the standard outcome measure — reconviction within two years — captures only a fraction of what restorative conferencing is supposed to achieve. Victims who report a better sense of closure, communities that experience fewer informal tensions and offenders who develop a clearer awareness of harm caused do not show up in reconviction statistics. Hoyle does not dismiss the quantitative work; she suggests rather that the field has allowed reconviction to crowd out outcomes that are arguably more central to the practice's original aims.

These three positions are not in direct conflict, yet they pull policy in different directions. If the priority is to reduce repeat offending, the trials suggest concentrating conferencing on a relatively narrow group of cases where the underlying conditions resemble those of the original studies. If the priority is broader social repair, the appropriate metrics are not in current administrative datasets, and require survey instruments designed for the purpose. The disagreement is, at root, about what the practice is for.

A separate critique has emerged from scholars of sentencing reform more generally. Professor Michael Tonry, working between the University of Minnesota and the University of Cambridge, has argued that the focus on individual interventions, however well evaluated, distracts attention from larger structural questions about the use of imprisonment. Tonry's body of comparative work suggests that custodial rates across high-income democracies vary by an order of magnitude — from roughly 60 prisoners per 100,000 residents in parts of Scandinavia to more than 600 in some American states — and that the variation reflects political and cultural choices rather than differences in underlying offending. From this vantage, restorative justice trials, even successful ones, address the wrong unit of analysis.

Defenders of the meta-analytic tradition have responded with some force. Strang, in particular, has rejected the suggestion that small effects are uninteresting effects. A 27 per cent reduction over two years, even confined to a particular subgroup, would represent a substantial public benefit if scaled across the offences in which it has been demonstrated. The methodological gold standard, in her view, is not the size of a single estimate but the consistency of estimates across independent trials, and on that criterion the conferencing literature compares favourably with the wider evaluation evidence in criminal justice.

Strip away the slogans and a narrower, sturdier finding remains. Offer conferencing to a suitable case — a willing victim, a trained facilitator, a young first-time offender — and the reoffending dial moves modestly downward while the victim's sense of resolution improves a great deal. Push the same room into harder territory, with a repeat offender or a history of domestic abuse, and the evidence thins almost to nothing. Recent European and North American juvenile trials echo the earlier numbers, yet the confidence intervals around them stay wide enough to swallow a small effect whole.

Set this finding beside Tonry's structural argument and a layered view of reform comes into focus. Restorative conferencing is unlikely on its own to transform sentencing patterns that are driven by political and cultural forces well beyond the courtroom; equally, it is unlikely to be without value as one element of a wider repertoire. The interesting question, in the writer's view, is not whether the practice works in some abstract sense but under what institutional conditions its modest, well-documented benefits can be reliably delivered to the cases that stand to gain most. A trial that answered that, rather than producing one more headline percentage, would be the one worth running next.

audio_scripts.text: Right, settle down. Today's tutorial — we've got Marwa and Tomas reporting on their restorative-justice fieldwork. Marwa, you wanna start? And for the recording, could you spell your surname?

Sure. Marwa Idris — that's I-D-R-I-S, no second I before the S. People sometimes write it as I-D-R-I-S-S with a double-S; mine is single. My project tracked sixty-four mediated victim-offender conferences across the Highfield Probation Trust. (Q1)

Erm, the intake started in 2020 — sorry, no, 2019 — and the analytic phase closed in 2023. So roughly four years end to end. Originally we'd planned to wrap up in 2022, but the courts backlog, you know, pushed everything back by twelve months. (Q2)
Okay. Just to clarify tense-wise for the recording — your conference data collection FINISHED in 2023, the working paper goes out this year, correct?
Right. Working paper 2026, but the replication study we're gonna launch begins in 2028.

Well, the dominant theoretical lens is what John Braithwaite called the "reintegrative shaming framework". And just to flag the terminology — you'll see related labels in the older literature: communitarian sanction, conferencing protocol, family group decision-making. All of these gesture toward overlapping practices. The current scholarly term, though, is reintegrative shaming. I'll stick with that. (Q3)

Yeah, and I'm gonna echo Marwa's framing. In my sample — forty-one juvenile cases across two North-American counties — most of the offenders said they felt the process was procedurally fair. Actually, sorry, let me be precise — thirty-one out of forty-one, so roughly seventy-six per cent. Only a few — about twelve per cent — described the process as humiliating, and some — about another twelve per cent — reported indifference. (Q4)
Right. Now, Marwa, did your sample confirm the "shame-deters-recidivism" hypothesis?

Sorta, yeah, but with caveats. Most of the offenders I interviewed did NOT report shame as the principal deterrent. The salient mechanism, well, was relational repair — the chance to meet the victim. Only a small minority — fewer than fifteen per cent — cited shame itself as the deciding factor. (Q5)

And, kinda interesting on the dosage axis — so-called intensive conferencing, where mediators stage multiple follow-ups across six months, that's actually rising sharply in higher-resource jurisdictions. The evaluation literature suggests dosage correlates with desistance.
Hmm. Marwa, did you stratify by offence severity?
We did. Counter-intuitively, the LOWEST-severity bracket reported the highest perceived legitimacy of the process, not the most serious offences.
Well, it's about expectation calibration — low-severity offenders expect punitive treatment and find the mediated route disproportionately respectful.

And one final point — repeat-offending rates. In smaller probation cohorts of under thirty cases, recidivism variance was, um, considerably higher than in larger cohorts of fifty-plus. Statisticians attribute it to small-sample noise.

Right. Now, going back to what Marwa mentioned at the start — that "current scholarly term" — that's the construct we'll operationalise next week. Oh, and Tomas, on your seventy-six-per-cent figure: the implication that perceived procedural fairness is high aligns with Braithwaite, but Marwa's relational-repair finding qualifies it. Good tension. Thanks both. (Q6)

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: Contemporary debates over criminal policy frequently pit reformist models against punitive ones. While certain commentators insist that restorative justice yields better outcomes than locking offenders away, others maintain that punishment must remain the cornerstone of any credible system. Personally, I lean toward the rehabilitative camp, although I concede that incarceration retains a residual function.

Proponents of restorative justice argue, in the main, that traditional incarceration tends to be criminogenic rather than corrective. Stripped of employment prospects and burdened with social stigma, ex-convicts frequently slide back into crime — a pattern reflected in recidivism rates exceeding fifty per cent in numerous jurisdictions. It is precisely this revolving-door dynamic that mediated dialogue, victim compensation and community service appear to interrupt, since they compel perpetrators to confront the human cost of their actions. Juvenile delinquents in particular, driven by guilt rather than resentment, tend to respond constructively when given the chance to make amends to their victims.

On the other side, advocates of harsh sentencing emphasise general deterrence and public safety. They argue, not unreasonably, that the credible threat of a long custodial term may dissuade would-be offenders from committing serious felonies in the first place. Furthermore, victims and their families, who have often suffered greatly, expect the courts to deliver proportionate retribution rather than leniency. For genuinely dangerous criminals, moreover, physical incapacitation behind bars is the only reliable way to protect the wider community.

In my view, however, evidence broadly favours the restorative approach for non-violent crimes, whereas incarceration should be reserved for genuinely dangerous individuals. By combining vocational training with mediated accountability, governments are more likely to break the cycle of reoffending and reduce overall victimisation in the long run, rather than merely recycling offenders through ever more crowded institutions.

Few questions in criminology divide opinion as sharply as whether restorative justice outperforms custodial punishment, or whether deterrence must take precedence. Although both philosophies have a legitimate place, the available evidence suggests that a rehabilitative paradigm produces more durable reductions in offending, with imprisonment reserved for the most serious felonies.

Defenders of restorative justice contend, with considerable empirical support, that conventional incarceration is itself criminogenic. Once labelled and warehoused, offenders typically emerge with diminished employability and intensified social stigma, conditions under which recidivism becomes almost predictable. So damaging is this churn that some Nordic jurisdictions have all but dismantled large prisons in favour of mediated dialogue, restitution and structured community sanctions. By foregrounding the victim's voice and demanding accountability from the perpetrator, such interventions appear to foster a moral re-engagement that a custodial term seldom achieves.

By contrast, retributivists argue that punishment vindicates the rule of law and signals society's moral censure. The threat of a long sentence, they suggest, may serve as a meaningful deterrent for instrumentally rational offenders, while the physical incapacitation of violent criminals demonstrably prevents further harm. Not without merit is the observation that, for heinous offences such as homicide or terrorism, restorative procedures would strike most citizens as derisory and re-traumatising for grieving families. A justice system perceived as toothless, they add, risks eroding public confidence in the rule of law altogether.

In my view, the dichotomy is overstated. The most defensible architecture is graduated: restorative pathways for misdemeanours, juvenile delinquency and non-violent felonies, complemented by proportionate incarceration for the genuinely dangerous. Only by integrating reintegration programmes — vocational training, mental-health support and post-release supervision — can states meaningfully arrest the cycle of reoffending. Under such an arrangement, the penal system would punish, deter and rehabilitate simultaneously, rather than collapsing these aims into a single, blunt instrument of confinement.

Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. High rates of recidivism suggest that many people who go to prison end up committing another crime after they get out. — RECIDIVISM (n, không đếm được) = sự tái phạm; collocation thường gặp "a high rate of recidivism", "reduce/curb recidivism". Tránh viết "a recidivism" hay "recidivisms".

2. Some experts doubt that long prison terms actually act as an effective deterrent to crime. — DETERRENT (n) = yếu tố răn đe; collocation chuẩn là "act as a deterrent TO something", không dùng giới từ "for". Phân biệt với "deterrence" (khái niệm răn đe nói chung, trừu tượng hơn).

3. The heinous nature of the attack disturbed even experienced police officers. — HEINOUS (adj) = tàn bạo, ghê tởm đến mức gây sốc; thường đi với "crime/act/nature of something". Chỉ dùng cho hành vi cực kỳ nghiêm trọng, không dùng cho lỗi nhỏ.

4. Breaking into someone's house and stealing their belongings is a felony, not a minor offence. — FELONY (n) = trọng tội (phạt tù trên 1 năm); đối lập với "misdemeanour" (tội nhẹ). Học viên hay nhầm hai từ này khi phân loại mức độ nghiêm trọng của tội.

5. It is extremely difficult for a former prisoner to achieve full reintegration into society after release. — REINTEGRATION (n) = sự tái hoà nhập cộng đồng; collocation "reintegration into society", "a reintegration programme". Gốc "re- + integrate" giúp ghi nhớ nghĩa "hoà nhập trở lại".

6. Detectives spent months trying to identify the perpetrator of the crime. — PERPETRATOR (n) = thủ phạm, người trực tiếp gây án; collocation "the perpetrator of a crime", "identify/bring the perpetrator to justice". Đối lập với "victim" (nạn nhân).

7. Many criminologists believe that prisons should focus on the rehabilitation of offenders rather than simply punishing them. — REHABILITATION (n, không đếm được) = sự cải tạo; collocation "focus on rehabilitation", "rehabilitation, not retribution". Không nói "a rehabilitation".

8. Because it was his first offence, the court decided to give him a surprisingly lenient sentence. — LENIENT (adj) = khoan dung, nhẹ tay; collocation "a lenient sentence/judge". Đối lập với "strict/harsh". Danh từ liên quan là "leniency".

9. Years later, new evidence revealed that the man's conviction had been a miscarriage of justice. — MISCARRIAGE OF JUSTICE (n phrase) = án oan, sự bất công trong xét xử; collocation "a serious miscarriage of justice", "a victim of a miscarriage of justice". Đồng nghĩa "wrongful conviction".

10. In some neighbourhoods where the police are slow to respond, ordinary residents have started acting as vigilantes. — VIGILANTE (n) = người tự đứng ra thực thi pháp luật ngoài khuôn khổ chính thức; dễ nhầm về mặt chữ với "vigilant" (cảnh giác, tính từ) — hai từ không liên quan về nghĩa.

11. Critics argue that the new law is punitive rather than aimed at addressing the causes of offending. — PUNITIVE (adj) = mang tính trừng phạt; collocation "a punitive approach/measures". Đối lập với "rehabilitative/restorative".

12. Given how much damage the fraud caused, many felt that the company had merely been given a slap on the wrist. — A SLAP ON THE WRIST (idiom) = hình phạt rất nhẹ, mang tính cảnh cáo, không tương xứng với mức độ nghiêm trọng; thường dùng với động từ "get/give", không nói "do a slap on the wrist".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu
1. Band 7: Simply increasing the prison population does not automatically make communities safer.
Band 8: Expanding custodial capacity is no guarantee of public safety, particularly when overcrowded prisons do little to curb recidivism.
2. Band 7: Judges need to weigh the circumstances carefully before imposing an unusually long sentence.
Band 8: Sentencing decisions warrant careful judicial discretion, since disproportionately lengthy custodial terms can prove more punitive than proportionate.
3. Band 7: Juvenile offenders should be dealt with differently from adult criminals within the justice system.
Band 8: Cases of juvenile delinquency arguably demand a distinct legal framework, given that young offenders are generally more amenable to rehabilitation than their adult counterparts.
4. Band 7: Many believe that white-collar offenders often escape the severe punishment their crimes deserve.

Band 8: There is a widespread perception that white-collar criminals are treated with disproportionate leniency, receiving little more than a slap on the wrist for offences that inflict substantial harm.
5. Band 7: Public confidence in the legal system tends to suffer whenever a prominent case is mishandled.
Band 8: Public confidence in the judiciary can be irreparably damaged whenever a high-profile miscarriage of justice comes to light.
6. Band 7: Supporting ex-offenders in securing steady employment can prevent them from reoffending.
Band 8: Facilitating stable employment for former prisoners is instrumental in easing their reintegration into society and curbing recidivism.
7. Band 7: A court's verdict on guilt should always rest on solid, thoroughly examined evidence.
Band 8: Any verdict reached by a jury ought to be grounded in rigorously scrutinised evidence, lest an avoidable miscarriage of justice ensue.
8. Band 7: Some argue that prisons themselves can turn minor offenders into more serious criminals.
Band 8: Critics contend that custodial environments are themselves criminogenic, transforming petty offenders into hardened criminals rather than reforming them.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)
High Recidivism Rates: In many countries, over 50% of released prisoners reoffend within 3 years due to social stigma and a lack of employment opportunities.
Overcrowded Prisons: Mass incarceration policies have led to prisons operating at 120-150% capacity, creating unsafe environments that hinder rehabilitation.
Rise of Cybercrime: A modern form of white-collar crime that transcends international borders, making perpetrators incredibly difficult to track and prosecute.
The Cost of Incarceration: Housing a prisoner costs taxpayers tens of thousands of dollars annually, prompting governments to consider community service for petty crimes.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: The Purpose of Prisons (Punishment vs. Rehabilitation)

For Punishment (Retribution/Deterrent): Ensures safety for law-abiding citizens by removing dangerous individuals from the streets; provides closure and justice for victims' families; strict consequences deter potential criminals.

For Rehabilitation: Most prisoners will eventually be released, so they must be reformed to protect future society; treating addiction and providing vocational training tackles the root causes of crime; ultimately cheaper than endless cycles of incarceration.
Topic: Fixed Punishments vs. Case-by-Case Assessment
Fixed Punishments (Pros): Ensures equality under the law (no discrimination based on wealth or race); speeds up the judicial process and saves court time; acts as a clear, predictable deterrent.

Case-by-Case (Pros): Allows judges to consider mitigating circumstances (e.g., self-defence, mental illness, poverty); more humane and flexible; separates hardened criminals from desperate, first-time offenders.
Topic: Capital Punishment (The Death Penalty)
Arguments FOR: The ultimate deterrent for heinous crimes; saves taxpayer money compared to life imprisonment; prevents the absolute worst perpetrators from ever reoffending.

Arguments AGAINST: The irreversible risk of executing innocent people (wrongful convictions); violates fundamental human rights; statistics show it does not lower murder rates more effectively than life in prison.

Cue card: Describe a law that you think should be changed. You should say: what the law is; why it exists in its current form; how it could be changed; and explain why you think this change is necessary.
Model Answer (≈ 268 words, Band 7.5–8.0):

The piece of legislation I would most readily overhaul is Vietnam's drug-possession statute under Article 249 of the Penal Code, which still treats personal use of narcotics — even minute quantities — as a criminal offence punishable by mandatory incarceration. What strikes me about this framework is that it is fundamentally criminogenic rather than rehabilitative: by funnelling first-time users into overcrowded prisons, the state effectively manufactures recidivism instead of addressing the underlying pathology of addiction.

The rationale, historically, was retribution and deterrence — the assumption being that harsh penalties would dissuade experimentation. Yet decades of empirical evidence point in the opposite direction. Portugal's 2001 decriminalisation reform, arguably the most rigorous natural experiment in this space, slashed problematic drug use by roughly half while HIV transmission among injecting users plummeted. Such data, it seems to me, fundamentally undermines the deterrent argument.

What I would propose is a pivot towards a restorative-justice model: personal possession would be reclassified as a misdemeanour triggering mandatory treatment, vocational training and community service, rather than imprisonment. Trafficking, naturally, would remain a felony. Underpinning this shift is the recognition that addiction is, at its core, a public-health issue masquerading as a criminal one.

The reason this reform matters so much to me is twofold. Firstly, Vietnam's recidivism rate hovers above 50%, which suggests the punitive paradigm is demonstrably failing. Secondly — and this is what really clinches it — having watched a family acquaintance cycle through three custodial sentences without ever receiving counselling, I am convinced that what these individuals need is reintegration, not stigmatisation. Were such a reform enacted, both fiscal savings and human dignity would, I believe, be substantially recovered.

blocks.text: Q1: Should drug policy focus on harm reduction rather than criminalisation?

I'd argue rather strongly that it should, though with calibrated caveats. The harm-reduction paradigm — encompassing needle-exchange schemes, supervised consumption sites and opioid-substitution therapy — has accumulated a fairly robust evidence base. Switzerland's heroin-assisted treatment programme, for instance, has been credited with reducing drug-related crime by approximately 60% among enrolled participants since the 1990s. What this suggests is that criminalisation tends to push users underground, exacerbating the very harms it purports to prevent. That said, I wouldn't go so far as to advocate blanket legalisation; trafficking and supply-side offences clearly warrant punitive measures. The sweet spot, in my view, lies in decoupling personal use from criminal liability while doubling down on enforcement against organised networks. Were governments to embrace this hybrid model, public-health metrics would, in all likelihood, improve dramatically.
Q2: Are prisons effective at reducing crime?

Honestly, the evidence here is rather damning. Far from acting as a deterrent, mass incarceration appears to function as a finishing school for criminality — what criminologists term the "schools-of-crime" effect. Take the United States, where over two million people are behind bars yet recidivism within five years exceeds 75%. What that figure really tells us is that prison isolates offenders from prosocial networks while immersing them in criminogenic environments. Norway's Halden Prison, conversely, prioritises rehabilitation and vocational training, and its recidivism sits at roughly 20%. The lesson, I think, is unambiguous: prisons may be necessary for incapacitating violent perpetrators, but as a general response to crime, they are spectacularly inefficient. A graduated system blending probation, restorative justice and selective incarceration would, in my judgement, deliver far superior outcomes at a fraction of the fiscal cost.
Q3: Can community policing genuinely work?

In principle, yes — provided several preconditions are met. Community policing, at its essence, reframes officers as embedded problem-solvers rather than reactive enforcers, and the evidence from Glasgow's Violence Reduction Unit is genuinely encouraging: homicide rates there were halved over a decade through a public-health approach to gang violence. What makes the model work is the cultivation of legitimacy — residents must perceive the police as accountable partners, not occupying forces. Where it tends to falter is in contexts of entrenched mistrust or systemic corruption, where surface-level outreach cannot paper over structural dysfunction. Furthermore, community policing demands sustained investment in training, language skills and de-escalation — resources that cash-strapped municipalities often lack. So while I'm cautiously optimistic, I'd stress that it's no panacea; it's one component of a broader rehabilitative ecosystem, and its success hinges critically on political will.

4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good morning. Today's lecture interrogates three intertwined pillars of contemporary criminology: restorative justice, mass incarceration and the criminogenic factors that fuel reoffending. The carceral orthodoxy, I will contend, is empirically discredited.

> Consider, first, mass incarceration. The United States, with under five percent of the world's population, warehouses roughly twenty percent of its prisoners. The Princeton sociologist Bruce Western has documented how punitive sentencing, the so-called "war on drugs", and disinvestment from public housing converged in the 1980s to produce what he terms a carceral underclass. Prisons, far from neutralising deviance, frequently amplify it — concentrating trauma, severing kinship ties, and entrenching unemployment upon release.

> Now, criminogenic factors. The Cambridge longitudinal study, directed by David Farrington, tracked four hundred and eleven boys across half a century. The strongest predictors of adult offending were not innate pathology but socioeconomic deprivation, parental neglect and school exclusion. Crime, in short, is manufactured upstream of the courtroom; prosecuting downstream merely launders the failure.

> Finally, restorative justice. Pioneered in New Zealand's family-group conferencing model from 1989, the paradigm convenes offender, victim and community to negotiate reparation and accountability. A meta-analysis by Lawrence Sherman, published in 2015, found restorative interventions reduced recidivism by approximately twenty-seven percent relative to conventional sentencing — while improving victim satisfaction. The mechanism is unsentimental: confronting harm cultivates empathy that punishment cannot manufacture.

Right, figure two. Before we read the trend lines, I want to pre-empt the objection that's no doubt forming in some of your minds: didn't crime fall in the very decades when incarceration soared? Surely, then, prison works? Well, this is where we must be forensic. The National Research Council's landmark 2014 report disaggregated exactly this. They concluded that the fourfold rise in American imprisonment accounted for, at most, a modest fraction — somewhere between ten and twenty-five per cent — of the crime decline, and that the marginal deterrent value collapsed sharply beyond a certain threshold. In plain terms, the first prison cell may buy some public safety; the millionth buys almost none, while the social costs keep mounting. [pause]

A further consideration is what criminologists call the "replacement effect", particularly in drug markets. Incarcerate a street-level dealer, and the lucrative vacancy is filled within days — sometimes hours — by another, often younger, recruit. You have, if you like, churned a human being through the carceral machine without denting supply at all. The enterprise was never neutralised; merely a name on the org chart changed. [pause]

What complicates the restorative picture, in fairness, is scalability. Sherman's twenty-seven per cent reduction is genuinely impressive, but the New Zealand conferencing model is labour-intensive, facilitator-dependent, and culturally embedded in ways that resist mechanical export. Bolt it onto an adversarial, overloaded court system as a tick-box exercise, and the empathy mechanism — the very thing that does the work — evaporates. Implementation fidelity, um, is everything. [pause]

So when we plot imprisonment against violent crime here, notice that the two lines diverge precisely where theory predicts: more cages, flat or rising harm. The carceral reflex, I'd submit, is not merely cruel but fiscally incontinent. And that divergence sets up the harder question for legislators — let me flag the key policy implication…

> The synthesis is uncomfortable for policymakers: prisons should be the residuum, not the reflex. Without addressing criminogenic upstream conditions and embedding restorative practice, recidivism is mathematically guaranteed. Now, turning to figure two, which plots imprisonment rates against violent-crime trends since 1970…

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~289 words)

Contemporary debates over criminal policy frequently pit reformist models against punitive ones. While certain commentators insist that restorative justice yields better outcomes than locking offenders away, others maintain that punishment must remain the cornerstone of any credible system. Personally, I lean toward the rehabilitative camp, although I concede that incarceration retains a residual function.

Proponents of restorative justice argue, in the main, that traditional incarceration tends to be criminogenic rather than corrective. Stripped of employment prospects and burdened with social stigma, ex-convicts frequently slide back into crime — a pattern reflected in recidivism rates exceeding fifty per cent in numerous jurisdictions. It is precisely this revolving-door dynamic that mediated dialogue, victim compensation and community service appear to interrupt, since they compel perpetrators to confront the human cost of their actions. Juvenile delinquents in particular, driven by guilt rather than resentment, tend to respond constructively when given the chance to make amends to their victims.

On the other side, advocates of harsh sentencing emphasise general deterrence and public safety. They argue, not unreasonably, that the credible threat of a long custodial term may dissuade would-be offenders from committing serious felonies in the first place. Furthermore, victims and their families, who have often suffered greatly, expect the courts to deliver proportionate retribution rather than leniency. For genuinely dangerous criminals, moreover, physical incapacitation behind bars is the only reliable way to protect the wider community.

In my view, however, evidence broadly favours the restorative approach for non-violent crimes, whereas incarceration should be reserved for genuinely dangerous individuals. By combining vocational training with mediated accountability, governments are more likely to break the cycle of reoffending and reduce overall victimisation in the long run, rather than merely recycling offenders through ever more crowded institutions.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~304 words)

Few questions in criminology divide opinion as sharply as whether restorative justice outperforms custodial punishment, or whether deterrence must take precedence. Although both philosophies have a legitimate place, the available evidence suggests that a rehabilitative paradigm produces more durable reductions in offending, with imprisonment reserved for the most serious felonies.

Defenders of restorative justice contend, with considerable empirical support, that conventional incarceration is itself criminogenic. Once labelled and warehoused, offenders typically emerge with diminished employability and intensified social stigma, conditions under which recidivism becomes almost predictable. So damaging is this churn that some Nordic jurisdictions have all but dismantled large prisons in favour of mediated dialogue, restitution and structured community sanctions. By foregrounding the victim's voice and demanding accountability from the perpetrator, such interventions appear to foster a moral re-engagement that a custodial term seldom achieves.

By contrast, retributivists argue that punishment vindicates the rule of law and signals society's moral censure. The threat of a long sentence, they suggest, may serve as a meaningful deterrent for instrumentally rational offenders, while the physical incapacitation of violent criminals demonstrably prevents further harm. Not without merit is the observation that, for heinous offences such as homicide or terrorism, restorative procedures would strike most citizens as derisory and re-traumatising for grieving families. A justice system perceived as toothless, they add, risks eroding public confidence in the rule of law altogether.

In my view, the dichotomy is overstated. The most defensible architecture is graduated: restorative pathways for misdemeanours, juvenile delinquency and non-violent felonies, complemented by proportionate incarceration for the genuinely dangerous. Only by integrating reintegration programmes — vocational training, mental-health support and post-release supervision — can states meaningfully arrest the cycle of reoffending. Under such an arrangement, the penal system would punish, deter and rehabilitate simultaneously, rather than collapsing these aims into a single, blunt instrument of confinement.

•  Band 8 đưa lập trường phân tầng tinh tế ('graduated architecture' với phân loại tội cụ thể) và bác bỏ thế lưỡng phân ('the dichotomy is overstated'), nâng Task Response so với Band 7 vốn chỉ nghiêng một phía.

•  Band 8 dùng đảo ngữ cao cấp ('So damaging is this churn that...', 'Not without merit is the observation...') và nominalisation dày ('the physical incapacitation of violent criminals', 'moral re-engagement'), trong khi Band 7 chủ yếu câu phức thường.

•  Band 8 lexis chuyên ngành tội phạm học sâu hơn ('warehoused', 'moral censure', 'instrumentally rational', 'derisory', 'restitution', 'graduated architecture') và cohesion liền mạch, tránh cụm đời thường ('locking offenders away', 'leniency') còn ở Band 7.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự tái phạm của tội phạm sau khi ra tù hoặc bị xử phạt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> High levels of **recidivism** indicate that criminals are not being successfully reformed.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
re- (lại) + cid (rơi, ngã, gốc Latin "cadere") → "ngã lại vào tội lỗi" → tái phạm.
vocabulary.common_error: Recidivism là danh từ trừu tượng, không đếm được — tránh viết 'a recidivism' hay 'recidivisms'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the tendency of a convicted criminal to reoffend after being released or punished
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự tái phạm (của tội phạm sau khi ra tù)
vocabulary.example: High levels of recidivism indicate that criminals are not being successfully reformed.
vocabulary.memory_hook: re- (lại) + cid (rơi, ngã, gốc Latin 'cadere') → 'ngã lại vào tội lỗi' → tái phạm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Yếu tố hoặc biện pháp có tác dụng răn đe, ngăn chặn hành vi phạm tội.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many people argue that strict prison sentences do not act as an effective **deterrent**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
de- (tránh xa) + terr (sợ hãi, như "terror") → thứ khiến người ta sợ mà tránh xa → răn đe.
collocations: act as a deterrent to crime
vocabulary.common_error: 'Deterrent' (danh từ/tính từ chỉ yếu tố răn đe) khác với 'deterrence' (danh từ trừu tượng chỉ khái niệm/chính sách răn đe nói chung).
vocabulary.definition_en: something that discourages a person from doing something, especially through fear of the consequences
vocabulary.definition_vi: yếu tố răn đe
vocabulary.example: Many people argue that strict prison sentences do not act as an effective deterrent.
vocabulary.memory_hook: de- (tránh xa) + terr (sợ hãi, như 'terror') → thứ khiến người ta sợ mà tránh xa → răn đe.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự giam giữ hoặc bỏ tù một người trong cơ sở giam giữ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Mass **incarceration** policies have led to prisons operating at 120-150% capacity, creating unsafe environments that hinder rehabilitation.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
in- (vào trong) + carcer (nhà tù, gốc Latin "carcer") → nhốt vào trong nhà tù → sự giam giữ.
vocabulary.common_error: *Incarceration* là danh từ không đếm được trong nghĩa chung; dùng *a period of incarceration*, không nói *an incarceration policy* khi muốn nói chính sách bỏ tù hàng loạt.
vocabulary.definition_en: the act of imprisoning or confining someone in a penal institution
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự giam giữ, sự bỏ tù
vocabulary.example: Mass incarceration policies have led to prisons operating at 120-150% capacity, creating unsafe environments that hinder rehabilitation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: in- (vào trong) + carcer (nhà tù, gốc Latin 'carcer') → nhốt vào trong nhà tù → sự giam giữ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cực kỳ tàn bạo, ghê tởm, độc ác đến mức gây sốc — thường dùng để mô tả tội ác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The public was absolutely shocked by the **heinous** nature of the murder.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Nghe gần giống "hateness" (sự căm ghét) → tội ác khiến người ta căm ghét, ghê tởm.
vocabulary.common_error: *Heinous* chủ yếu mô tả tội ác/hành vi cực kỳ độc ác; không dùng như từ cường điệu chung cho một việc chỉ hơi tệ.
vocabulary.definition_en: utterly odious, wicked, or evil to a shocking degree, typically describing a crime
vocabulary.definition_vi: tàn bạo, ghê tởm, cực kỳ độc ác (thường mô tả tội ác)
vocabulary.example: The public was absolutely shocked by the heinous nature of the murder.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Nghe gần giống 'hateness' (sự căm ghét) → tội ác khiến người ta căm ghét, ghê tởm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trọng tội — tội hình sự nghiêm trọng, thường bị phạt tù trên một năm.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He committed a **felony** and was sentenced to ten years' incarceration.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Felony nghe như "fell on you" → tội nặng "giáng xuống" đời bạn → trọng tội.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'felony' (trọng tội, >1 năm tù) với 'misdemeanour' (tội nhẹ, như shoplifting).
vocabulary.definition_en: a serious criminal offence, typically punishable by more than one year of imprisonment
vocabulary.definition_vi: trọng tội
vocabulary.example: He committed a felony and was sentenced to ten years' incarceration.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Felony nghe như 'fell on you' → tội nặng 'giáng xuống' đời bạn → trọng tội.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hệ thống tư pháp tập trung hàn gắn tổn hại bằng cách để người phạm tội, nạn nhân và cộng đồng cùng tham gia, thay vì chỉ trừng phạt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Restorative justice** compels offenders to confront the human cost of their actions.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
restore (phục hồi) + justice (công lý) → công lý nhằm phục hồi, hàn gắn, không chỉ trừng phạt.
vocabulary.common_error: Không nhầm *restorative justice* với việc giảm án đơn thuần; trọng tâm là sửa chữa tổn hại với nạn nhân, người phạm tội và cộng đồng.
vocabulary.definition_en: a system of criminal justice focused on repairing harm by involving offenders, victims, and the community, rather than solely punishing
vocabulary.definition_vi: tư pháp phục hồi
vocabulary.example: Restorative justice compels offenders to confront the human cost of their actions.
vocabulary.memory_hook: restore (phục hồi) + justice (công lý) → công lý nhằm phục hồi, hàn gắn, không chỉ trừng phạt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá trình giúp cựu tù nhân quay trở lại và hòa nhập hiệu quả với xã hội chính thống.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It's very hard for people leaving prison to achieve full **reintegration** into society.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
re- (lại) + integrate (hòa nhập) → hòa nhập trở lại xã hội sau khi ra tù.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *reintegration into society/the community*, không phải *reintegration to society*.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of helping ex-offenders return to and function effectively within mainstream society
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự tái hòa nhập (cộng đồng)
vocabulary.example: It's very hard for people leaving prison to achieve full reintegration into society.
vocabulary.memory_hook: re- (lại) + integrate (hòa nhập) → hòa nhập trở lại xã hội sau khi ra tù.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thủ phạm — người thực hiện một hành vi gây hại, phi pháp hoặc phi đạo đức.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The police are still searching for the **perpetrator** of the bank robbery.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
perpetrate (thực hiện hành vi xấu) + -or (người) → người thực hiện tội ác → thủ phạm.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *the perpetrator of a crime/attack*; không dùng cho nạn nhân và không nhầm với *prosecutor*.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person who carries out a harmful, illegal, or immoral act
vocabulary.definition_vi: thủ phạm, kẻ gây án
vocabulary.example: The police are still searching for the perpetrator of the bank robbery.
vocabulary.memory_hook: perpetrate (thực hiện hành vi xấu) + -or (người) → người thực hiện tội ác → thủ phạm.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá trình giúp người phạm tội quay lại cuộc sống lành mạnh, tuân thủ pháp luật thông qua giáo dục, trị liệu, đào tạo nghề.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The main goal of the prison system should be the **rehabilitation** of offenders.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
re- (lại) + habilis (có năng lực, gốc Latin) → làm cho có năng lực trở lại → cải tạo.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong ngữ cảnh hình sự, *rehabilitation* là cải tạo người phạm tội; không nhầm với *reintegration*, tức giai đoạn tái hòa nhập xã hội.
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of restoring an offender to a useful, law-abiding life through education, therapy, or training
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự cải tạo, phục hồi (chức năng, nhân cách)
vocabulary.example: The main goal of the prison system should be the rehabilitation of offenders.
vocabulary.memory_hook: re- (lại) + habilis (có năng lực, gốc Latin) → làm cho có năng lực trở lại → cải tạo.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Khoan dung, nhẹ tay hơn dự kiến — thường mô tả một bản án hoặc hình phạt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The judge gave him a surprisingly **lenient** sentence because it was a minor, first-time offence.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Lenient nghe gần "leniency" (sự nhẹ nhàng) → hình dung một quan tòa mỉm cười, nhẹ tay.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *lenient with somebody* hoặc *lenient towards/on something*; không nhầm với *lenitive*.
vocabulary.definition_en: more merciful or tolerant than expected, especially in the severity of a punishment
vocabulary.definition_vi: khoan dung, nhẹ tay (trong xử phạt)
vocabulary.example: The judge gave him a surprisingly lenient sentence because it was a minor, first-time offence.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Lenient nghe gần 'lenient = leniency = nhẹ nhàng' → hình dung một quan tòa mỉm cười, nhẹ tay.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tình huống tòa án đưa ra phán quyết sai hoặc bất công, đặc biệt là kết án oan người vô tội.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Miscarriages of justice**, though relatively rare, can irreparably damage public confidence in the legal system.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
miscarriage (sự thất bại, hỏng) + of justice (của công lý) → công lý bị "hỏng", xử sai → án oan.
collocations: a victim of a miscarriage of justice
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm cố định là *a miscarriage of justice*; không dùng *miscarriage in justice* và không hiểu theo nghĩa y khoa của *miscarriage*.
vocabulary.definition_en: a situation in which a court makes an unfair or wrong decision, especially convicting an innocent person
vocabulary.definition_vi: án oan, sự bất công trong xét xử
vocabulary.example: Miscarriages of justice, though relatively rare, can irreparably damage public confidence in the legal system.
vocabulary.memory_hook: miscarriage (sự thất bại, hỏng) + of justice (của công lý) → công lý bị 'hỏng', xử sai → án oan.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Người tự đứng ra thực thi pháp luật mà không có thẩm quyền hợp pháp, thường khi cảnh sát hoạt động kém hiệu quả.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> In areas with weak policing, **vigilante** justice can escalate into mob violence against suspected criminals.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Gốc Tây Ban Nha "vigilante" = người canh gác → tự đứng ra canh gác, thực thi công lý riêng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Vigilante' (người tự xử) khác với 'vigilant' (cảnh giác, tính từ) — hai từ không liên quan về nghĩa dù giống mặt chữ.
vocabulary.definition_en: a person who takes law enforcement into their own hands without legal authority, typically in the absence of effective policing
vocabulary.definition_vi: người tự thực thi luật pháp (ngoài vòng pháp luật chính thức)
vocabulary.example: In areas with weak policing, vigilante justice can escalate into mob violence against suspected criminals.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Gốc Tây Ban Nha 'vigilante' = người canh gác → tự đứng ra canh gác, thực thi công lý riêng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Liên quan đến việc giam giữ hoặc bị quản thúc chính thức.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Custodial** sentences alone often fail to address the root causes of offending, doing little to curb recidivism.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
custody (sự giam giữ, quyền giám hộ) + -al (tính từ) → thuộc về sự giam giữ.
vocabulary.common_error: Trong luật hình sự, *custodial sentence* là án tù; không dùng *custodial* một mình để thay cho *imprisonment*.
vocabulary.definition_en: relating to imprisonment or being kept in official custody
vocabulary.definition_vi: liên quan đến việc giam giữ
vocabulary.example: Custodial sentences alone often fail to address the root causes of offending, doing little to curb recidivism.
vocabulary.memory_hook: custody (sự giam giữ, quyền giám hộ) + -al (tính từ) → thuộc về sự giam giữ.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Mang tính trừng phạt, nhằm mục đích trừng trị thay vì cải tạo.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The government just wants to adopt a **punitive** approach instead of helping offenders through rehabilitation.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
punitive gần với "punish" (trừng phạt) → mang tính trừng phạt.
vocabulary.common_error: *Punitive* nghĩa là nhằm trừng phạt và thường đi với *measures, damages, approach*; không đồng nghĩa hoàn toàn với *strict*.
vocabulary.definition_en: intended as punishment rather than reform or reward
vocabulary.definition_vi: mang tính trừng phạt
vocabulary.example: The government just wants to adopt a punitive approach instead of helping offenders through rehabilitation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: punitive gần với 'punish' (trừng phạt) → mang tính trừng phạt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự trừng phạt mang tính đền tội hoặc báo thù cho một hành vi sai trái.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The rationale, historically, was **retribution** and deterrence — the assumption being that harsh penalties would dissuade experimentation.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
re- (lại, đáp trả) + tribut (cống nạp, trả) → trả lại tương xứng cho tội đã gây ra → trừng phạt.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'retribution' (trừng phạt mang tính báo thù/đền tội, danh từ trừu tượng) với 'contribution' — khác gốc và nghĩa hoàn toàn.
vocabulary.definition_en: punishment inflicted on someone as vengeance for a wrong or criminal act
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự trừng phạt (mang tính báo thù, đền tội)
vocabulary.example: The rationale, historically, was retribution and deterrence — the assumption being that harsh penalties would dissuade experimentation.
vocabulary.memory_hook: re- (lại, đáp trả) + tribut (cống nạp, trả) → trả lại tương xứng cho tội đã gây ra → trừng phạt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hành vi phạm tội hoặc chống đối xã hội do người vị thành niên thực hiện.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> This is particularly crucial for cases of **juvenile delinquency**, where young offenders can still be reformed with proper guidance.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
juvenile (trẻ vị thành niên) + delinquency (hành vi phạm pháp) → tội phạm ở tuổi vị thành niên.
vocabulary.common_error: *Juvenile delinquency* thường là danh từ không đếm được chỉ hiện tượng; không gọi một cá nhân là *a juvenile delinquency*—dùng *juvenile delinquent*.
vocabulary.definition_en: criminal or antisocial behaviour committed by young people, typically minors
vocabulary.definition_vi: tội phạm vị thành niên
vocabulary.example: This is particularly crucial for cases of juvenile delinquency, where young offenders can still be reformed with proper guidance.
vocabulary.memory_hook: juvenile (trẻ vị thành niên) + delinquency (hành vi phạm pháp) → tội phạm ở tuổi vị thành niên.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bị bắt quả tang khi đang thực hiện hành vi sai trái hoặc phạm pháp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The thief couldn't deny the crime because he was **caught red-handed** with the stolen goods.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
red-handed = "tay dính máu/màu đỏ" → hình ảnh kẻ trộm bị bắt lúc tay còn dính "tang vật" → bắt quả tang.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *be caught red-handed doing something*; không nói *caught with red hands* và lưu ý đây là văn phong thân mật.
vocabulary.definition_en: caught in the act of doing something wrong or illegal, with clear evidence of guilt
vocabulary.definition_vi: bị bắt quả tang
vocabulary.example: The thief couldn't deny the crime because he was caught red-handed with the stolen goods.
vocabulary.memory_hook: red-handed = 'tay dính máu/màu đỏ' → hình ảnh kẻ trộm bị bắt lúc tay còn dính 'tang vật' → bắt quả tang.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Trừng phạt ai đó nghiêm khắc nhất có thể, áp dụng mức hình phạt tối đa.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The judge wanted to make an example of the corrupt politician, so he decided to **throw the book at** him.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"the book" = cuốn luật hình sự đầy đủ mọi tội danh → "ném" cả cuốn sách luật vào ai đó = xử nặng hết mức.
collocations: the judge threw the book at him
vocabulary.common_error: Mẫu cố định là *throw the book at someone*; đại từ tân ngữ đứng cuối, không đặt giữa *throw* và *the book*.
vocabulary.definition_en: to punish someone as severely as possible, imposing the maximum penalty allowed
vocabulary.definition_vi: trừng phạt ai đó nặng nhất có thể, xử theo khung hình phạt tối đa
vocabulary.example: The judge wanted to make an example of the corrupt politician, so he decided to throw the book at him.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'the book' = cuốn luật hình sự đầy đủ mọi tội danh → 'ném' cả cuốn sách luật vào ai đó = xử nặng hết mức.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cố tình làm ngơ, phớt lờ một hành vi sai trái hoặc phạm pháp mà mình biết rõ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Authorities were accused of **turning a blind eye** to the illegal logging happening in the forest.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"blind eye" = con mắt mù → cố tình "mù" trước sai phạm để khỏi phải xử lý.
collocations: turn a blind eye to something
turn a blind eye to corruption
vocabulary.common_error: Giới từ bắt buộc là *to*: *turn a blind eye to corruption*; không dùng *on* hoặc bỏ giới từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: to deliberately ignore something wrong or illegal that one is aware of
vocabulary.definition_vi: làm ngơ, cố tình nhắm mắt cho qua
vocabulary.example: Authorities were accused of turning a blind eye to the illegal logging happening in the forest.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'blind eye' = con mắt mù → cố tình 'mù' trước sai phạm để khỏi phải xử lý.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Làm điều sai trái hoặc phạm pháp mà không bị bắt hay trừng phạt.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> He is the boss's son, so he can break all the company rules and **get away with** it.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"get away" (thoát đi) + "with" (mang theo) → mang theo tội lỗi mà vẫn thoát thân → thoát tội.
collocations: let someone get away with it
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *get away with + noun/V-ing*; *murder* có thể là nghĩa bóng “không bị phạt”, nên tránh trong văn học thuật trang trọng nếu dễ gây mơ hồ.
vocabulary.definition_en: to do something wrong or illegal without being caught or punished for it
vocabulary.definition_vi: thoát tội, làm sai mà không bị trừng phạt
vocabulary.example: He is the boss's son, so he can break all the company rules and get away with it.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'get away' (thoát đi) + 'with' (mang theo) → mang theo tội lỗi mà vẫn thoát thân → thoát tội.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Một lần va chạm nhẹ, ngắn ngủi với cảnh sát hoặc hệ thống pháp luật.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Although he is a respected doctor now, he had **a brief brush with the law** when he was a teenager.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"brush" = chạm nhẹ, lướt qua → chỉ va chạm thoáng qua với pháp luật, không nghiêm trọng.
collocations: a brief brush with the police
vocabulary.common_error: Cụm cố định là *a brush with the law*; không nói *a brush of the law* và thường chỉ một va chạm nhỏ với pháp luật.
vocabulary.definition_en: a brief or minor encounter with the police or legal system
vocabulary.definition_vi: một lần va chạm nhẹ với pháp luật
vocabulary.example: Although he is a respected doctor now, he had a brief brush with the law when he was a teenager.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'brush' = chạm nhẹ, lướt qua → chỉ va chạm thoáng qua với pháp luật, không nghiêm trọng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hình phạt rất nhẹ, mang tính nhắc nhở, không tương xứng với mức độ nghiêm trọng của hành vi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> For a minor offence like speeding, you usually just get **a slap on the wrist**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
"slap on the wrist" = đánh nhẹ vào cổ tay như cách người lớn nhắc trẻ con → phạt qua loa, không đau.
collocations: get a slap on the wrist
just a slap on the wrist
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *a slap on the wrist* cho hình phạt quá nhẹ; không nhầm với hành động đánh thật và không dùng *in the wrist*.
vocabulary.definition_en: a very mild punishment that is much less severe than the offence might warrant
vocabulary.definition_vi: hình phạt nhẹ, mang tính cảnh cáo
vocabulary.example: For a minor offence like speeding, you usually just get a slap on the wrist.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'slap on the wrist' = đánh nhẹ vào cổ tay như cách người lớn nhắc trẻ con → phạt qua loa, không đau.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bồi thẩm đoàn đưa ra phán quyết chính thức về việc bị cáo có tội hay vô tội.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> After three days of intense deliberation, the jury finally **reached a guilty verdict**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
verdict gốc Latin "vere dictum" = "nói thật, nói đúng" → lời tuyên bố cuối cùng của bồi thẩm đoàn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Verdict' (phán quyết của bồi thẩm đoàn về có tội hay không) khác với 'sentence' (mức án cụ thể do thẩm phán tuyên sau đó).
vocabulary.definition_en: for a jury to arrive at a formal decision on whether a defendant is guilty or innocent
vocabulary.definition_vi: đưa ra phán quyết (có tội)
vocabulary.example: After three days of intense deliberation, the jury finally reached a guilty verdict.
vocabulary.memory_hook: verdict gốc Latin 'vere dictum' = 'nói thật, nói đúng' → lời tuyên bố cuối cùng của bồi thẩm đoàn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Có xu hướng tạo ra hoặc thúc đẩy hành vi phạm tội, thường mô tả các điều kiện cấu trúc hoặc môi trường.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Critics argue that mass incarceration is itself **criminogenic** rather than corrective.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
crimino- (tội phạm) + -genic (sinh ra, như "photogenic") → thứ "sinh ra" tội phạm.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Criminogenic' mô tả nguyên nhân/điều kiện sinh ra tội phạm, không dùng để mô tả bản thân một tội phạm cụ thể hay một người ('a criminogenic person' là sai).
vocabulary.definition_en: tending to produce or encourage criminal behaviour, typically referring to structural or environmental conditions
vocabulary.definition_vi: có tính sinh ra tội phạm (mô tả điều kiện/môi trường)
vocabulary.example: Critics argue that mass incarceration is itself criminogenic rather than corrective.
vocabulary.memory_hook: crimino- (tội phạm) + -genic (sinh ra, như 'photogenic') → thứ 'sinh ra' tội phạm.
